elements.quote: Importantly however, high rates of poor mental health are common in clinical staff working in acute medicine generally [3-5] and so estimating the additional impact of epidemic and pandemic response, not solely the extent of poor mental health, is also important in guiding decisions to protect staff mental health. Given that the SARS-CoV-2/COVID-19 pandemic is likely to evolve in location, course and severity over time, traditional meta-analyses are only likely to give a snapshot of the current state of the evidence.
elements.reason: Describes current knowledge on mental health in clinical staff and uncertainties due to evolving pandemic.

elements.quote: Consequently, we report a rapid review and meta-analysis that forms the basis of a living meta-analysis of the mental health of clinical staff dealing with epidemics and pandemics of high-risk infectious diseases, including studies from coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), Ebola virus disease, H1N1 influenza, severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), and middle east respiratory syndrome (MERS) to understand the potential impact on mental health and to inform policy on supporting staff during the current COVID-19 pandemic.
elements.reason: Explains the importance and need for the review to estimate additional burden and inform policy.

elements.quote: Recently, a meta-analysis by Kisely et al. [6] reported that healthcare workers in direct contact with affected patients had an approximately 1.71-1.74 odds ratio of reporting acute mental health problems compared to healthcare workers not in direct contact with infected patients. Given that the SARS-CoV-2/COVID-19 pandemic is likely to evolve in location, course and severity over time, traditional meta-analyses are only likely to give a snapshot of the current state of the evidence. Living systematic reviews or meta-analyses are a new innovation that allow estimates to be updated as new evidence emerges [7, 8] but have rarely been used to date.
elements.reason: Cites previous review and explains need for current living meta-analysis due to evolving evidence.
The review assesses mental health outcomes, not intervention effects.
The review does not involve complex interventions, so a logic model is not applicable.

elements.quote: Due to studies using differing cut-offs for determining caseness even when using the same scale, meta-analysis for prevalence was not possible. However, two types of meta-analytic estimates were possible: a comparison of risk ratios for studies that compared above-cut off scoring between high- and low-exposure groups, and meta-analysis for differences in mean scale scores between high and low exposures.
elements.reason: The choice of risk ratios for prevalence differences and standardised mean differences for mean score differences is justified based on data availability and study design constraints.
